title: Unit 2: Monera, Protoctista and Fungi
blurb: Based on Anaya pages 52 to 61: bacteria, protozoa, algae and fungi.
sort: Its cells are prokaryotic and unicellular
Its most abundant group is the bacteria
It is classified by shape: cocci, bacilli, vibrios, spirilla and spirochaeta
It reproduces asexually only, by binary fission
Its cyanobacteria photosynthesise without having chloroplasts
It can live in the most extreme temperatures, acidity and salinity
Some of its members twist, spin or slide over surfaces to move
Its symbiotic types include the bacteria of the gut microbiota
It is classified into four groups: ciliates, flagellates, rhizopods and sporozoans
Its rhizopods move and capture food with pseudopods
Its ciliates have tiny moving filaments called cilia on the surface
Its sporozoans are parasites with a simple structure and no way of moving
It helps to treat sewage by feeding on decomposer bacteria
It is a unicellular, heterotrophic eukaryote with no cell wall
Its cells have chloroplasts containing chlorophyll, and a cell wall
It is autotrophic and lives in aquatic environments
It can be unicellular, colony-forming or multicellular
It is classified as green, red or brown according to its pigments
Multicellular ones have a holdfast to attach to rocks and gas bladders to float
Some of it causes red tides by producing toxins
Agar, a food thickener, is extracted from it
Multicellular ones reproduce by alternation of generations (sporophyte and gametophyte)
It has a cell wall, no chloroplasts, and feeds heterotrophically on organic matter
Its body is a mycelium made of filaments called hyphae
Its groups include yeasts, moulds and mushroom-forming fungi
Its unicellular members reproduce by budding
Lichens are formed by one of these living together with an alga
Some of it produces antibiotics, and some causes athlete's foot and ringworm
The mushroom is its reproductive structure, and the mycelium is buried underground
Truffles and saffron milk caps are valued in cooking

cloze: Monera are {prokaryotic~a} and {unicellular~a} organisms that can be autotrophic or heterotrophic.
Bacteria are classified by shape: {cocci} are spherical, {bacilli} are rod-shaped and {vibrios} are comma-shaped.
Bacteria reproduce asexually by {binary fission}: the cell makes a copy of its {DNA}, narrows in the middle and makes two {daughter} cells.
Protozoa are classified into four groups: ciliates, flagellates, {rhizopods~a} and {sporozoans~a}.
Rhizopods move and capture food using projections of the cytoplasm called {pseudopods}.
Algae are {autotrophic} because their {chloroplasts} contain a pigment called {chlorophyll}.
Depending on their pigments, algae can be green, {red~a} or {brown~a}.
Multicellular algae reproduce by alternation of generations: the {sporophyte} makes spores and the {gametophyte} makes gametes.
The body of a multicellular fungus is the {mycelium}, made of filaments called {hyphae}.
Yeasts reproduce by {budding}, while multicellular fungi reproduce through {spores}.
A {lichen} is a symbiosis between a fungus and an alga.
{Saprophytic} fungi break down organic matter in the ground and form {humus}.

clues: I have no chloroplasts, so I am heterotrophic.
I move with tiny filaments called cilia.
I move and capture food with pseudopods, my false feet.
I move with a single filament that I wave like a whip.
I have a simple structure, I cannot move, and I form spores.
I am a kind of bacterium.
My shape is an elongated spiral.
I attach to rocks with a rhizoid and I can be green, red or brown.
I have a cell wall but no chloroplasts.
My body is a mycelium buried underground, and my cap makes spores.

order.title: Binary fission in bacteria
steps: The bacterium grows and makes a copy of its DNA
The bacterium narrows in the middle and divides its contents

order.title: Budding in a yeast
steps: The yeast cell forms a small bud
The bud separates from the cell
A new daughter cell is formed

order.title: Alternation of generations in a multicellular alga
steps: The spores germinate into male and female gametophytes
The gametophytes make male and female gametes
The male and female gametes join in fertilisation
The zygote grows into a new sporophyte

order.title: A mushroom-forming fungus
steps: Spores fall from the gills of the mushroom
A spore germinates and grows hyphae underground
The hyphae join together to form the mycelium
A mushroom grows up from the mycelium to make new spores

explain.q: Describe the main characteristics of Monera.
points: They are unicellular
They are prokaryotes
Their nutrition is autotrophic or heterotrophic
They reproduce asexually through binary fission
The largest group is the bacteria
explain.hint: Cover the number of cells, the type of cell, how they feed, how they reproduce and the biggest group.

explain.q: How are Monera classified? Name the groups.
points: They are classified by their shape
Cocci
Bacilli
Vibrios
Spirochaeta
explain.hint: Say what we use to classify them, then name the four shapes.

explain.q: Describe how bacteria reproduce.
points: Asexually
By binary fission
A mother cell divides
Two daughter cells are produced
explain.hint: Think about the type of reproduction, its name, and what you start with and end with.

explain.q: Describe the main characteristics of protozoa.
points: They are unicellular
They are eukaryotes
Their nutrition is heterotrophic
They reproduce asexually, and some reproduce sexually through gametes
explain.hint: Cover the number of cells, the type of cell, how they feed and how they reproduce.

explain.q: How are protozoa classified? What does each group use to move?
points: They are classified by how they move around
Ciliates use cilia
Flagellates use a flagellum
Rhizopods use pseudopods
explain.hint: Say what we use to classify them, then name three groups and what each one moves with.

explain.q: Describe the main characteristics of algae.
points: They are unicellular or multicellular
They are eukaryotes
Their cells have chloroplasts and a cell wall
Their nutrition is autotrophic
explain.hint: Cover the number of cells, the type of cell, the cell parts and how they feed.

explain.q: Describe the different kinds of algae and where they live.
points: Unicellular algae: free forms or colonies
Multicellular algae can be green, red or brown
Multicellular algae are attached to the sea floor or river bed
explain.hint: Think about unicellular and multicellular algae separately: what forms they take, their colours and where they live.

explain.q: How do algae reproduce?
points: Asexually: binary fission, fragmentation or spores
Sexually: through gametes
explain.hint: Two types of reproduction. Give the ways for the first one and the way for the second.

explain.q: Describe the main characteristics of fungi.
points: They are unicellular or multicellular
They are eukaryotes
Their cells have a cell wall but no chloroplasts
Their nutrition is heterotrophic
They are generally attached to the ground or other living things
explain.hint: Cover the number of cells, the type of cell, the cell parts, how they feed and where they live.

explain.q: How are fungi classified?
points: Yeasts: unicellular
Moulds: they grow on food
Mushroom-forming fungi
explain.hint: Name the three groups and say one thing that identifies each.

explain.q: What is the body of a fungus called, and what is it made of?
points: The body is called the mycelium
It is a collection of hyphae
In mushrooms, the fruiting body produces the spores
explain.hint: Name the body, say what it is made of, and think about the part of a mushroom that makes spores.

explain.q: How do fungi reproduce?
points: Asexually
Unicellular fungi (yeasts) reproduce by budding
Multicellular fungi reproduce through spores
explain.hint: The type of reproduction first, then the way for unicellular fungi and the way for multicellular fungi.

explain.q: Compare algae and fungi.
points: Both are eukaryotes with a cell wall
Both can be unicellular or multicellular
Algae have chloroplasts and are autotrophic
Fungi have no chloroplasts and are heterotrophic
explain.hint: Say two things they share and two things that are different (think about chloroplasts and feeding).

explain.q: Compare Monera and Protoctista.
points: Monera are prokaryotes; Protoctista (protozoa and algae) are eukaryotes
Monera are unicellular; algae can be multicellular
Monera reproduce by binary fission; protozoa reproduce asexually, and some sexually
Protoctista are the simple eukaryotes
explain.hint: Think about the type of cell, the number of cells and the way they reproduce.

explain.q: For each group (Monera, protozoa, algae, fungi), say whether it is autotrophic or heterotrophic.
points: Monera: autotrophic or heterotrophic
Protozoa: heterotrophic
Algae: autotrophic
Fungi: heterotrophic
explain.hint: Four groups, four answers. Only one of them can be either.

explain.q: How do bacteria feed?
points: They have no organelles such as chloroplasts or mitochondria, so all nutrition takes place in the cytoplasm
Autotrophic bacteria make their own organic matter by photosynthesis
Heterotrophic bacteria feed on the organic matter of other living beings
Saprophytic (decomposer) bacteria feed on remains of organic matter
Symbiotic bacteria form a mutually beneficial relationship; parasitic bacteria take organic matter and cause harm
explain.hint: Think about the different ways bacteria can get their food (4 or 5 types) and give an example of each. Remember they have no organelles.

explain.q: Describe the process of bacterial binary fission.
points: The bacterium grows to a sufficient size
It makes a copy of its genetic material (DNA)
It narrows in the middle and divides its contents
Two daughter cells are produced
explain.hint: Think of it as a sequence: what happens to the bacterium first, what happens to its genetic material, then how it splits. How many cells at the end?

explain.q: Explain how protozoa feed.
points: Protozoa are heterotrophic
Some are parasitic: they consume the organic matter of the living beings they live in and cause disease
Others feed on organic matter, bacteria and other protoctista
explain.hint: What kind of feeders are protozoa (autotroph or heterotroph)? Then think of two different sources of food: living hosts, and organic matter in the environment.

explain.q: Describe the structures that allow some protozoa to move around.
points: Cilia: tiny moving filaments on the surface (ciliates)
A flagellum: a single filament that moves like a whip (flagellates)
Pseudopods: projections of the cytoplasm, or false feet (rhizopods)
Sporozoans have no movement structures
explain.hint: Name each structure and say what it looks like and which group has it. One group has no movement structure at all.

explain.q: How are algae classified?
points: By cellular complexity: unicellular, colony-forming or multicellular
By pigments: green algae contain mostly chlorophyll
Red algae contain red pigments
Brown algae contain orange pigments
explain.hint: Think of the different ways to sort algae: by how complex their cells are, and by the colour of their pigments. Give the colours.

explain.q: Explain how algae reproduce.
points: Asexually: binary fission, fragmentation (a new individual from a fragment) or spores
Sexually, through gametes
Some multicellular algae alternate between sexual and asexual reproduction (alternation of generations)
The sporophyte is the asexual phase and the gametophyte is the sexual phase
explain.hint: Two main ways: without gametes and with gametes. Give examples of the asexual ways, and mention the cycle some multicellular algae follow.

explain.q: Explain how fungi interact.
points: Unicellular fungi can live independently or grow on fruits, plants and so on
Mushroom-forming fungi live attached to the ground
Some live in symbiosis, as in lichens (a fungus and an alga)
explain.hint: Think of three ways fungi live: alone, attached to something, and in partnership with another organism. Give an example of the partnership.

explain.q: How are bacteria helpful and harmful to humans?
points: Helpful: the bacteria in our bodies help us function
Helpful: decomposer bacteria treat sewage and waste; photosynthetic bacteria oxygenate water and air; fermentative bacteria make cheese, yoghurt and vinegar
Harmful: some cause diseases such as tetanus and salmonellosis
Harmful: others contaminate food and spoil it
explain.hint: Two lists: good things bacteria do for us (inside our bodies, in sewage and in nature) and bad things (disease and food). Give an example of each.

explain.q: How are protozoa helpful and harmful to humans?
points: Helpful: they are used in sewage treatment by feeding on decomposer bacteria
Helpful: they make up plankton, food for many aquatic organisms that humans eat
Harmful: parasitic protozoa cause diseases such as malaria (spread by mosquito bites)
Harmful: and amebiasis (spread through water or contaminated food)
explain.hint: Two lists: good things protozoa do (sewage, food chains) and harm they cause (diseases, and how they spread). Name the diseases.

explain.q: How are algae helpful and harmful to humans?
points: Helpful: they oxygenate the oceans and atmosphere and consume carbon dioxide
Helpful: they are food for protozoa and aquatic organisms, and for humans
Helpful: they are used as fertiliser and cattle feed, and agar is extracted from them
Harmful: some cause red tides, producing toxins that can reach humans through contaminated fish
explain.hint: Two lists: how algae help (oxygen, food, fertiliser, industry) and how they can harm (red tides). Say what red tides do.

explain.q: How are fungi helpful and harmful to humans?
points: Helpful: saprophytic fungi form humus on which plants feed
Helpful: some mushrooms, such as truffles and saffron milk caps, are valued in cooking
Helpful: moulds produce antibiotics and other drugs; yeasts make alcoholic drinks and bread
Harmful: parasitic fungi cause athlete's foot and ringworm, and infect plants and damage crops
Harmful: toxins from some mushrooms can be fatal
explain.hint: Two lists: how fungi help (soil, food, medicine) and how they harm (infections, toxins). Give an example for each.

explain.q: Give the main characteristics of Monera.
points: Prokaryotic and unicellular
Autotrophic or heterotrophic
Classified by shape: cocci, bacilli, vibrios, spirilla and spirochaeta
Reproduce asexually by binary fission
The most abundant group is the bacteria
explain.hint: Cover the cell type, the number of cells, how they feed, how they are classified, how they reproduce, and the commonest group.

explain.q: Give the main characteristics of protozoa.
points: Eukaryotic, unicellular and heterotrophic
Live in aquatic environments, moist earth or inside other living beings
Four groups: ciliates, flagellates, rhizopods and sporozoans
Reproduce mostly asexually (duplicate DNA, divide into two daughter cells); some sexually through gametes
explain.hint: Cover the cell type, how they feed, where they live, the four groups and how they reproduce.

explain.q: Give the main characteristics of algae.
points: Eukaryotic, autotrophic, living in aquatic environments
Unicellular, colony-forming or multicellular
Cell wall and chloroplasts containing chlorophyll
Green, red or brown according to their pigments
Reproduce asexually (fission, fragmentation, spores) or sexually (gametes)
explain.hint: Cover the cell type, how they feed, where they live, how complex they can be, their cell parts, colours and reproduction.

explain.q: Give the main characteristics of fungi.
points: Eukaryotic, heterotrophic, unicellular or multicellular
Cell wall (different from plants) and no chloroplasts
Live in moist, warm places protected from light
Multicellular fungi have hyphae that form the mycelium
Yeasts reproduce by budding; multicellular fungi by spores
explain.hint: Cover the cell type, how they feed, cell parts, the body structure of multicellular fungi and how yeasts and others reproduce.

explain.q: Explain what it means that bacteria are able to adapt to all environments.
points: They can live in every environment: water, land and air
They can live inside other living beings
They can survive the most extreme temperatures, acidity levels and salinity levels
explain.hint: Think about all the places bacteria can live, including inside other living things, and the extremes of temperature they can survive.

explain.q: Some Monera, such as cyanobacteria, photosynthesise. Bacteria have no chloroplasts, so where does this happen?
points: Bacteria have no organelles such as chloroplasts or mitochondria
All their nutrition processes take place in the cytoplasm
So photosynthesis takes place in the cytoplasm of the cell
explain.hint: Remember what bacteria do not have. Then think about where their processes happen instead, and so where photosynthesis must happen.

explain.q: Explain what would happen for humans if protozoa disappeared.
points: Many aquatic organisms that humans eat feed on plankton, which includes protozoa
Sewage treatment would be less effective, because protozoa feed on the decomposer bacteria it contains
Diseases such as malaria and amebiasis would no longer be caused by protozoa
explain.hint: Think about what humans would lose: food chains, sewage treatment, and what would happen to diseases. Say whether each effect is good or bad.

explain.q: Explain the difference between multicellular algae and colonial algae, if both are formed by grouping non-tissue-forming cells.
points: Colonial algae are unicellular algae that live together as a colony (for example Volvox and Pandorina)
Multicellular algae are one organism with structures for attaching and floating (phylloid, cauloid, rhizoid and gas bladders)
Examples of multicellular algae: sea lettuce and Gracilaria
explain.hint: Compare them: what are the cells like in each, and are they separate or one single organism? Give an example of the multicellular type.

explain.q: Imagine that algae suddenly disappeared from the waters of our planet. Explain what could happen.
points: Less oxygen would be produced for the oceans and the atmosphere
More carbon dioxide would be left, because algae consume large amounts of it
Protozoa and many aquatic organisms would lose their food
Humans would lose algae as food, fertiliser, cattle feed and agar
explain.hint: Think about the effect on the atmosphere (oxygen and carbon dioxide), the effect on other organisms in the water that depend on algae, and the effect on humans.

explain.q: Explain what a hypha and the mycelium of a fungus are.
points: A hypha is a filament-like structure formed by the cells of a multicellular fungus
Strands of hyphae join together to form the mycelium
The mycelium is the body of the fungus (in mushroom-forming fungi it is buried in the ground)
explain.hint: Say what each word means, what shape they have, and how they relate to each other. The mycelium is the body.

explain.q: In a lichen: which living beings are connected, and what does each provide to the other?
points: A lichen is a symbiosis between a fungus and an alga
The fungus provides the moist environment that the alga needs in order to live
The alga provides the food that the fungus needs (by photosynthesis)
explain.hint: Name the two living things, then say what each one gives the other.

explain.q: Would it be possible to find algae in the depths of the ocean? Give reasons.
points: Probably not: algae are autotrophic and make their food by photosynthesis
Photosynthesis needs light, which does not reach the depths of the ocean
Algae live in aquatic environments where there is enough light
explain.hint: Think about what algae need to make food and whether the deep ocean has it. Give your reason, not only yes or no.

Bacteria: photosynthetic ones that oxygenate water and the atmosphere
Bacteria: the ones that contaminate food and spoil it
Bacteria: decomposer bacteria used to treat sewage and waste

Protozoa: the ones that feed on decomposer bacteria in sewage treatment
Protozoa: the ones that cause malaria and amebiasis

items.why: They feed on the organic matter of other living beings, bacteria and other protoctista.

items.q: All protozoa live separately from other living beings.
items.why: Some are parasitic and live inside other living beings.

items.q: Protozoa cannot move around.
items.why: Many can: cilia, flagella and pseudopods are used to move. Sporozoans cannot.

items.q: Protozoa only reproduce asexually.
items.why: Some reproduce sexually through gametes.

items.q: Protozoa have a cell wall.
items.why: Protozoa do not have a cell wall.

items.q: All algae are multicellular and visible to the naked eye.
items.why: Many are unicellular and microscopic.

items.q: Red algae do not have chlorophyll as a photosynthetic pigment.
items.why: All algae have chlorophyll. Red algae also have red pigments.

items.q: Freshwater algae do not exist: all algae are marine algae.
items.why: Algae live in aquatic environments, which include fresh water.

items.q: All bacteria cause diseases.
items.why: The majority of bacteria are helpful.

items.q: Algae only reproduce asexually.
items.why: They can also reproduce sexually through gametes.

items.q: Since they perform photosynthesis, fungi live in dry, sunny places.
items.why: Fungi do not photosynthesise. They are heterotrophic and live in moist, warm places protected from light.

items.q: Fungi can cause diseases in humans, but never in plants.
items.why: Parasitic fungi also infect plants and damage crops.

items.q: Bacteria reproduce asexually by binary fission.
items.why: The single cell divides into two.

items.q: Bacteria have organelles such as chloroplasts and mitochondria.
items.why: They do not, so all their nutrition processes take place in the cytoplasm.

items.q: Algae are autotrophic.
items.why: They make their own organic matter through photosynthesis.

items.q: The mushroom of a mushroom-forming fungus is its reproductive structure.
items.why: The spores are made there. The mycelium is the buried body.

items.q: Fungi have the same kind of cell wall as plants.
items.why: The cell wall of a fungus is different from the cell wall of plants.

items.q: Yeasts are unicellular fungi.
items.why: They reproduce by budding.

items.q: Monera cells are eukaryotic.
items.why: Monera are prokaryotic.

items.q: Sporozoans get their name from the spores they form.
items.why: They form resistant structures called spores.

quizzes.name: Exam questions
quizzes.blurb: Multiple choice from the concept map and summary notes.

items.q: Monera are ...
items.why: Monera are unicellular and prokaryotes.

items.q: What is the largest group of Monera?
items.why: The largest group of Monera is the bacteria.

items.q: How do Monera reproduce?
items.why: Monera reproduce asexually through binary fission.

items.q: How do Monera get their food?
opts: Some are autotrophic and some are heterotrophic
items.a: Some are autotrophic and some are heterotrophic
items.why: Monera can be autotrophic or heterotrophic.

items.q: Monera are classified by their ...
items.why: We classify bacteria by their shape: cocci, bacilli, vibrios and spirochaeta.

items.q: Which of these is NOT a shape of bacteria?
items.why: The shapes are cocci, bacilli, vibrios and spirochaeta. Rhizopods are protozoa.

items.q: Binary fission makes ...
opts: two daughter cells from one mother cell
items.a: two daughter cells from one mother cell
items.why: A mother cell divides into two daughter cells.

items.q: How do bacteria move?
opts: They are attached to the sea floor
Some do not move and others move over surfaces
items.a: Some do not move and others move over surfaces
items.why: Some bacteria do not move and others move over surfaces.

items.q: Which kingdom has prokaryotes?
items.why: Monera are prokaryotes. Protoctista and Fungi are eukaryotes.

items.q: Protozoa are ...
items.why: Protozoa are unicellular eukaryotes.

items.q: How do protozoa get their food?
items.why: Protozoa are heterotrophic.

items.q: Protozoa are classified by ...
items.why: We classify protozoa by how they move around.

items.q: Which protozoa move using cilia?
items.why: Ciliates use cilia.

items.q: Which protozoa move using flagella?
items.why: Flagellates use a flagellum.

items.q: Which protozoa move using pseudopods?
items.why: Rhizopods use pseudopods.

items.q: How do protozoa reproduce?
opts: Asexually. Some also reproduce sexually through gametes
items.a: Asexually. Some also reproduce sexually through gametes
items.why: Protozoa reproduce asexually, and some reproduce sexually through gametes.

items.q: Algae are ...
items.why: Algae can be unicellular or multicellular, and they are eukaryotes.

items.q: How do algae get their food?
items.why: Algae are autotrophic.

items.q: Multicellular algae can be ...
items.why: Multicellular algae can be green, red or brown.

items.q: Algae cells have ...
opts: neither chloroplasts nor a cell wall
a cell wall but no chloroplasts
items.why: Algae cells have chloroplasts and a cell wall.

items.q: Where do multicellular algae live?
opts: Attached to the sea floor or river bed
items.a: Attached to the sea floor or river bed
items.why: Multicellular algae are attached to the sea floor or river bed.

items.q: Unicellular algae live as ...
items.why: Unicellular algae are free forms or colonies.

items.q: How do algae reproduce sexually?
items.why: Sexual reproduction in algae is through gametes.

items.q: Which is a way algae reproduce asexually?
items.why: Asexually: binary fission, fragmentation or spores.

items.q: Fungi are classified into ...
items.why: Fungi: yeasts, moulds and mushroom-forming fungi.

items.q: Which fungi are unicellular?
items.why: Yeasts are the unicellular fungi.

items.q: Moulds are fungi that ...
items.why: Moulds grow on food.

items.q: Fungal cells have ...
opts: a cell wall but no chloroplasts
items.a: a cell wall but no chloroplasts
items.why: Fungi have a cell wall but no chloroplasts.

items.q: The body of a fungus is called the ...
items.why: The body is the mycelium, a collection of hyphae.

items.q: The mycelium is made up of ...
items.why: The mycelium is made up of a collection of hyphae.

items.q: How do fungi get their food?
items.why: Fungi are heterotrophic.

items.q: Unicellular fungi reproduce by ...
items.why: Yeasts (unicellular) reproduce asexually by budding.

items.q: Multicellular fungi reproduce by ...
items.why: Multicellular fungi reproduce asexually through spores.

items.q: Fungi are generally ...
opts: able to make their own food
attached to the ground or other living things
items.a: attached to the ground or other living things
items.why: Fungi are generally attached to the ground or other living things.

items.q: Which kingdom includes protozoa and algae?
items.why: Protoctista includes the protozoa and the algae.

items.q: The concept map calls the Protoctista ...
items.why: Protoctista are the simple eukaryotes.

items.q: Which group has a cell wall and chloroplasts?
items.why: Algae have chloroplasts and a cell wall. Fungi have a cell wall but no chloroplasts.

quizzes.name: True or false (exam)
quizzes.blurb: True or false from the concept map and summary notes.

items.q: Monera are prokaryotes.
items.why: Monera are prokaryotes.

items.q: Monera are always multicellular.
items.why: Monera are unicellular.

items.q: Monera reproduce sexually through gametes.
items.why: Monera reproduce asexually through binary fission.

items.q: All Monera are heterotrophic.
items.why: Some are autotrophic and some are heterotrophic.

items.q: Vibrios and spirochaeta are shapes of bacteria.
items.why: We classify bacteria by their shape.

items.q: Protozoa are heterotrophic.
items.why: Protozoa are heterotrophic.

items.q: Protozoa are prokaryotes.
items.why: Protozoa are eukaryotes.

items.q: Ciliates move using cilia.
items.why: Ciliates use cilia.

items.q: Rhizopods move using flagella.
items.why: Rhizopods use pseudopods. Flagellates use flagella.

items.q: Some protozoa reproduce sexually through gametes.
items.why: Protozoa mostly reproduce asexually, and some use gametes.

items.q: Algae are autotrophic.
items.why: Algae make their own food.

items.q: All algae are unicellular.
items.why: Algae can be unicellular or multicellular.

items.q: Algae cells have chloroplasts and a cell wall.
items.why: Algae cells have chloroplasts and a cell wall.

items.q: Multicellular algae can be green, red or brown.
items.why: Green, red or brown.

items.q: Algae reproduce sexually through gametes.
items.why: Algae can reproduce asexually and sexually.

items.q: Algae reproduce by budding.
items.why: Budding is how yeasts reproduce. Algae use binary fission, fragmentation, spores or gametes.

items.q: Fungi are autotrophic.
items.why: Fungi are heterotrophic.

items.q: Fungal cells have chloroplasts.
items.why: Fungal cells have a cell wall but no chloroplasts.

items.q: The body of a fungus is called the mycelium.
items.why: The mycelium is a collection of hyphae.

items.q: Yeasts are unicellular.
items.why: Yeasts are the unicellular fungi.

items.q: Moulds grow on food.
items.why: Moulds grow on food.

items.q: Yeasts reproduce by budding.
items.why: Unicellular fungi reproduce by budding.

items.q: Multicellular fungi reproduce by binary fission.
items.why: Multicellular fungi reproduce through spores.

items.q: Fungi can be unicellular or multicellular.
items.why: Fungi can be unicellular or multicellular eukaryotes.

items.q: Which feature do fungi and plants share?
items.why: Both have a cell wall, but fungi have no chloroplasts, so they cannot photosynthesise.

items.q: What is the main difference between a fungus and an alga?
opts: Algae have chloroplasts and make their own food; fungi do not
Fungi have a nucleus; algae do not
items.a: Algae have chloroplasts and make their own food; fungi do not
items.why: Algae are autotrophs. Fungi are heterotrophs with no chloroplasts.

items.q: Which is NOT a way that fungi can get their food?
items.why: Fungi have no chloroplasts. They are saprophytic, parasitic or symbiotic.

items.q: A cell has a nucleus, a cell wall and no chloroplasts. What could it be?
items.why: A nucleus rules out bacteria; a cell wall rules out protozoa; no chloroplasts rules out algae.

items.q: What do fungi and bacteria have in common?
opts: Some are saprophytes that decompose dead matter
items.a: Some are saprophytes that decompose dead matter
items.why: Fungi are eukaryotes and bacteria are prokaryotes, but both include decomposers.

items.q: What is the difference between the hyphae and the mycelium?
opts: Hyphae are the filaments; the mycelium is the whole mass of them
Hyphae are the spores; the mycelium is the cap
The mycelium is a single hypha
items.a: Hyphae are the filaments; the mycelium is the whole mass of them
items.why: The mycelium is a collection of hyphae.

items.q: Which fungi cannot be seen as a single cell and reproduce by spores?
items.why: Yeasts are unicellular and bud; multicellular fungi make spores.

items.q: Why can a mushroom grow in a dark forest floor but an alga cannot?
opts: The fungus feeds on organic matter and does not need light
The fungus photosynthesises in the dark
items.a: The fungus feeds on organic matter and does not need light
items.why: Fungi are heterotrophs. Algae need light for photosynthesis.

items.q: In a lichen, what does the alga provide?
items.why: The fungus gives protection and water; the alga makes food.

items.q: Which of these is both a fungus and unicellular?
items.why: Yeasts are unicellular fungi. Amoeba is a protozoan.

items.q: A mould grows on bread. How is it feeding?
opts: It absorbs food from the bread (saprophytic)
It eats the bread with cilia
It is a parasite of the baker
items.a: It absorbs food from the bread (saprophytic)
items.why: Moulds are saprophytic fungi.

items.q: Which statement about the mushroom is correct?
opts: It is the reproductive structure; the body (mycelium) is underground
It is the whole body of the fungus
items.a: It is the reproductive structure; the body (mycelium) is underground
items.why: The mushroom makes spores; the mycelium is buried.
